Field Guide
Getting started
Before You Begin

Welcome to CargoDesk

CargoDesk is where you plan, book, and track ocean freight shipments — from the first price you quote a customer to the last invoice you reconcile. This guide walks you through processing one shipment from start to finish, in the order you'd actually do it.

1Sign in

Open CargoDesk in your browser and sign in with the email and password your administrator gave you. If you ever forget your password, use the Forgot password? link on the sign-in screen — don't ask a colleague to share theirs.

The sign-in screen — you'll land here every time your session expires.

2Get your bearings

Once you're in, you'll see the sidebar on the left and a "Good afternoon" home screen on the right. The sidebar is your map of the whole app — keep it open in the back of your mind as you go through this guide, since every chapter starts from one of these links.

  • Quotes — price a shipment for a customer before it's booked (Chapter 1)
  • Shipments — every shipment you've created or are working on (Chapter 2 onward)
  • Dashboard — how much container space you've used against what carriers gave you
  • Integration Board — the internal task board the CargoDesk team uses, not customer-facing
  • Schedule Search — a standalone sailing lookup, outside of any one shipment
  • AI Assistant — ask it about any shipment, contract, or allocation in plain English (Getting Help)

The home screen itself is worth a glance every morning: it shows your fleet-wide shipment counts, overdue milestones, and departures coming up in the next 7 days.

Home screen — the sidebar on the left is where every chapter in this guide begins.
💡

This guide follows one real shipment. Every screenshot from Chapter 2 onward shows the same example — a furniture importer, SHP-N02KYB, moving two containers of oak dining tables from Rotterdam to New York. Watch it pick up a carrier, a schedule, paperwork, and a price as you go — that's the point.

Chapter 1 of 10 · Optional starting point

Get a Quote

Not every shipment starts here — if you already know exactly what you're booking, skip ahead to Chapter 2. But if a customer is asking "how much to ship two containers from Rotterdam to New York," a Quote is where you answer that without committing to a real, numbered shipment yet.

1Open Quotes and start a new one

Click Quotes in the sidebar, then + New Quote. Fill in who you're quoting (search by company name or pick from the list), the route (POL/POD), and the carrier if you already know it.

The New Quote form — customer, route, cargo details, and pricing all live here.

2Price it

You have two ways to fill in the Quote Lines table at the bottom:

  • Type each charge in yourself — a service code like OF for Ocean Freight, a description, and a rate.
  • Click Find Matching Contracts to pull rates from a contract already on file for that route and carrier, then adjust them — the contract rate is usually your cost, so add your margin before saving.

Set a Valid Until date too — a quote needs one before you can send it, since an open-ended price isn't a real offer.

3Send it, then track the answer

Save the quote — it starts as a Draft, which you can still edit freely. When it's ready, open it and click Send to Customer. From here it moves to one of three places: the customer Accepts it, Declines it (with a reason, so you have a record), or it quietly Expires if nobody responds before the valid-until date.

An accepted quote — the only state where "Convert to Shipment" appears.

4Convert it to a real shipment

Once a quote is Accepted, click Convert to Shipment. CargoDesk creates a real, numbered shipment for you — same customer, same route, same carrier — and carries your quoted price over as the shipment's starting sell-side cost. You'll land straight on the new shipment's overview page, which is where Chapter 2 picks up.

SHP-N02KYB, seconds after conversion — this is our example shipment's very first moment.
ℹ

A quote's price doesn't have to match what you eventually pay the carrier. When the shipment is created, CargoDesk keeps the two sides separate on purpose — what you quoted the customer (sell) and what the carrier's contract actually charges (buy) — so your margin stays visible instead of getting averaged away. More on this in Chapter 10.

Chapter 2 of 10

Create the Shipment

A shipment is the one record everything else in this guide hangs off — cargo, booking, documents, and cost all attach to it. You'll get here one of two ways.

1Starting from an accepted quote

If you followed Chapter 1, you already have one — Convert to Shipment did this step for you. Nothing else to do here; skip to Chapter 3.

2Starting from scratch

From Shipments, click + New Shipment. At minimum CargoDesk needs at least one leg with a derived Port of Loading, Port of Discharge, and carrier, plus an Incoterm, a Commodity Code, and a Shipper/Consignee/Principal all set — everything else can be filled in later. Contract type isn't actually a gate on its own — it silently defaults to "SPOT," and only becomes a hard requirement (a real Contract ID) once you switch it to "Central."

Status update, verified 2026-08-25: corrects the original list above, which had this backwards — contract type was described as required and shipper/consignee/commodity/ Incoterm as optional-for-now; it's the other way around in the actual code.

The New Shipment form — POL, POD, carrier, and contract type are the only hard requirements.

3Know your shipment's home screen

Whichever path you took, you'll land on the shipment's Overview page. This is the dashboard for this one shipment — route, carrier, shipper/consignee, cargo value, and TEU count all summarized at the top, with the same info repeated as a header on every page you visit underneath it in the sidebar. Everything else in this guide happens through that left-hand sidebar, scoped to this one shipment.

SHP-N02KYB's Overview once cargo, parties, and a booking are all in place — where this chapter's shipment ends up by Chapter 6.
💡

Notice the sidebar below the shipment header — Cargo, Booking & Routing, Accounting, and so on. That's your table of contents for the rest of this shipment's life, and it's exactly the order this guide follows.

Chapter 3 of 10

Add Your Cargo

Before you can book a carrier or price anything properly, CargoDesk needs to know what's actually moving — how many containers, what size, and what's inside them.

1Add a container

Open Cargo in the shipment's sidebar and click + Add Container. Give it a container number if you have one already (the carrier will usually assign this once the booking is confirmed — it's fine to leave blank and fill in later), a size and type (a 40HC is a 40-foot high-cube, the most common), and — if you know the carrier's terms — how many free days you get at origin and destination before demurrage or detention charges start.

2Describe what's inside

Click into a container and add the cargo itself — pallets, boxes, or crates, each with a description, quantity, and value. This isn't busywork: the value you enter here is what feeds your customs filings, your commercial invoice, and the cargo-value figure shown on the shipment header.

Two 40HC containers, one carrying 18 crated oak dining tables — TEU and cargo value both update automatically as you go.
ℹ

TEU is calculated for you. A 20-foot container counts as 1 TEU, a 40-foot as 2 — add containers and the TEU total on the shipment header updates immediately, no manual math required.

Chapter 4 of 10

Find a Sailing

Before CargoDesk will let you book a carrier, it needs to know which sailing you're booking — this step is easy to skip past, but it's the one that unlocks Chapter 5.

1Add a route leg

Open Booking & Routing → Contracts & Schedules in the sidebar. If this is a simple port-to-port move, click + Add leg and confirm the POL, POD, and carrier — CargoDesk usually pre-fills these from the shipment itself.

One SEA leg, Rotterdam to New York on MAEU — this is what unlocks the "Add Sailing" search next to it.

2Search for a sailing and apply it

With a leg in place, Add Sailing becomes available. Search by the leg's own route and carrier, pick the sailing that fits your cargo-ready date, and apply it. CargoDesk copies the vessel name, voyage number, ETD, and ETA straight onto the shipment — you won't need to type any of that by hand.

⚠

This is a hard gate, not a suggestion. If you jump straight to Carrier Booking before a schedule (or a contract) is attached, CargoDesk stops you with a locked message rather than letting you send a booking request with no sailing behind it — you'll see exactly what that looks like at the start of the next chapter.

Chapter 5 of 10

Book the Carrier

With cargo and a sailing both in place, you're ready to actually reserve space with the carrier — CargoDesk calls this the carrier booking, and it's a real back-and-forth conversation, not a single button.

1What you'll see if you're not ready yet

Open Booking & Routing → Carrier Booking. If Chapter 4 isn't done yet, this is exactly what greets you instead of a booking form:

"This shipment doesn't have a contract or a schedule assigned yet." — go back and finish Chapter 4 first.

2Send the booking request

Once a schedule's attached, this page turns into a real form. Click Send Booking Request — CargoDesk sends the carrier an EDI message with your route, containers, cargo, and any dangerous-goods declaration bundled in automatically, so you don't retype anything you've already entered in earlier chapters.

3Wait for the carrier's response, then confirm

The booking sits as Pending until the carrier responds. Once they do — confirmed or rejected — you'll see their response logged with a raw/parsed payload toggle if you want to see exactly what came back. A confirmed response still needs one manual click, Confirm, where you record the carrier's own booking reference number. That reference is what shows up everywhere else in CargoDesk that refers to this booking.

ℹ

If you change the carrier on a leg after a booking already exists, CargoDesk doesn't edit the old one in place — it archives it (with a full history you can still see) and starts a fresh booking under the new carrier. A confirmed booking is treated as a historical fact and is never silently rewritten.

Chapter 6 of 10

Add Parties & Offices

A shipment involves more people than just you and the carrier. This chapter is about making sure everyone who needs to appear on a document or get notified is actually on record.

1The core four

Open Parties & Offices and click Edit. Every shipment has up to four fixed roles: Shipper, Consignee, Notify Party, and Principal (who CargoDesk is actually acting for — usually whichever side the Incoterm puts in charge). If you set these up already while creating the shipment, double-check them here.

2Everyone else

Underneath, Additional Parties covers forwarders, customs brokers (export and import are tracked separately, since they're routinely different companies), truckers, banks, and insurers. Add whichever ones apply — you'll need a broker on file before Chapter 7 will let you file customs paperwork.

Shipper, consignee, and notify party at the top; a forwarder and customs broker added below.
💡

Line agents fill themselves in. If the carrier has a registered local agent at your POL or POD, CargoDesk adds them automatically as soon as the shipment is created — you'll often find this section partly done for you already.

Chapter 7 of 10

Handle Customs

Depending on which side of the shipment you're responsible for, you may need to file with customs before the cargo can legally move. CargoDesk tracks two filing types side by side.

1Know which filing you need

  • AES/EEI (export) — needs a Customs Broker (Export) on the Parties page.
  • ISF/AMS (import) — needs a Customs Broker (Import) on the Parties page.

Both also need priced cargo already on the shipment — another reason Chapter 3 comes before this one.

2Create and submit the filing

Status update, verified 2026-08-25: since v0.72.0 the whole page is gated up front — it stays locked (both AES/EEI and ISF/AMS cards, no dismiss) until at least one broker is assigned, at least one priced cargo line exists, and both Shipper/USPPI and Consignee are set on Parties & Offices. Once past that gate, the per-side behavior below is accurate.

Open Customs Filing. Whichever side is missing its broker shows a greyed-out Create Filing button with a reminder of what to add first; the side that's ready lets you create and then Submit the filing straight away.

AES/EEI still waiting on an export broker; ISF/AMS already filed, submitted, and accepted.

3Track the response

A submitted filing sits as Filed until a response comes back — Accepted with a confirmation number, or rejected with a reason you can act on. Every message sent and received is logged right there on the card, so you never have to wonder whether something was actually submitted.

Chapter 8 of 10

Generate Documents

Everything you've entered so far — cargo, parties, booking, filings — feeds straight into the paperwork. You very rarely type a document by hand in CargoDesk; you generate it from what's already on file.

1Check what's still missing

Open Documents. The bar at the top tells you, at a glance, how many of this shipment's expected documents are confirmed, still drafts, or entirely missing — a Bill of Lading, a Commercial Invoice, a Packing List, and several more, all listed below it.

One Bill of Lading in Draft, everything else still Missing — click Generate next to any row to produce it.

2Generate, review, and confirm

Click Generate next to any missing document. CargoDesk builds it from the shipment's own data and produces a real, signed PDF — open it, check it over, and mark it Confirmed once it's ready to send. A confirmed document that later goes stale (say, the vessel changes after the B/L was issued) is flagged for you rather than silently left wrong.

Chapter 9 of 10

Track the Shipment

Once the cargo is actually moving, this is where you keep the record honest — logging what's happened, and seeing at a glance what's next.

1Log container events

Each container has its own movement history — Empty Pickup, Gate In, Loaded, Sailed, Discharged, Gate Out, Empty Return. Open a container from the Cargo page and log each stage as it happens — this is also what CargoDesk uses to calculate detention and demurrage later, so it's worth keeping current, not backfilled all at once.

2Work through the milestones

Open Milestones & Events. This is the shipment's overall timeline — Booking Confirmed, SI Submitted, Cargo Gated In, Vessel Departed, and on through to Delivered. Mark each one complete as it happens; the progress bar at the top gives you (and anyone else looking at this shipment) an instant read on how far along it is.

Booking Confirmed and Cargo Gated In are both done — 2 of 9 milestones complete.
ℹ

Completing things out of order won't block you. Real operations don't always happen in a tidy sequence — a carrier might confirm two updates the same day. CargoDesk flags an out-of-order completion so it's visible in the shipment's history, but it never stops you from recording what actually happened.

Chapter 10 of 10

Handle the Money

The last piece is making sure what you billed the customer, what the carrier billed you, and what you actually agreed to all line up. CargoDesk keeps these as three separate, connected views instead of one flat ledger.

1Cost Entry — what you owe

Open Accounting → Cost Entry. This is the buy side — every charge you owe a carrier or vendor, whether it came in automatically from a contract or you added it by hand with + Add Line.

Ocean Freight and Origin THC, both BUY-side — $1,370 total owed to the carrier.

2GP Overview — your margin, live

Accounting → GP Overview puts buy and sell side by side and does the subtraction for you — estimated and actual, so you can see immediately whether a shipment is on plan or has drifted.

Est. Buy
$1,370.00
Est. Sell
$1,630.00
$260 gross profit, a 16% margin — and a Prepaid/Collect breakdown showing who actually pays where.

3Freight Audit & Payment — trust, but verify

When the carrier's actual invoice arrives, don't just pay what it says. Open Freight Audit & Payment from the sidebar's Dashboard section and click + New Carrier Invoice. Enter each line from the carrier's invoice — CargoDesk automatically compares it against what you already accrued in Cost Entry (or the contract rate if nothing was accrued yet) and flags anything outside a normal tolerance.

Ocean Freight matched exactly; Origin THC came in $35 (15.9%) over what was accrued — flagged, not silently paid.

From here you Approve a line — which posts it as the real, actualized cost — or Dispute it if the charge looks wrong, keeping a record of why.

💡

Detention and demurrage get the same treatment. If a carrier bills you for late container return, CargoDesk independently recalculates what's actually owed from the container's own free-time window (Chapter 9) before comparing it to the carrier's number — so a padded D&D charge doesn't just sail through.

Before You Begin

Getting Help

You've now walked one shipment all the way from a quote to a reconciled invoice. A few more things worth knowing before you're on your own.

1Ask the AI Assistant

Click AI Assistant in the sidebar (or the icon in the top bar from any shipment) and ask it something plain, like "what's the status of SHP-N02KYB" or "list active shipments on MAEU." It can look up real shipments, contracts, and allocations for you — it just can't click buttons on your behalf, so use it for answers, not actions.

2Extract data from a document instead of retyping it

On the New Carrier Invoice form (Chapter 10), look for Extract from document — upload the carrier's invoice as a PDF or image and CargoDesk reads it and pre-fills the form for you. Always review what it pulled out before saving; treat it as a fast first draft, not the final word.

3Where to go from here

This guide covers the core path end to end, but CargoDesk does more than fits in one walkthrough — Master Data (carriers, ports, trade lanes), the Command Center, and the Integration Board among them. For a feature-by-feature reference rather than a step-by-step story, open User Manual from the user menu (the top-right avatar dropdown, not the left sidebar) — it's organized by topic instead of by sequence, so it's the right place to look something up once you already know your way around.

Status update, verified 2026-08-25: corrects "from the sidebar's footer" above — User Manual lives in the user-avatar dropdown menu, not the left nav rail.

🎉

That's the whole lifecycle — quote, shipment, cargo, schedule, booking, parties, customs, documents, tracking, and money. Every real shipment you process from here follows this same shape.
